desc:
Two strings of the same length are shift-equivalent if one is obtained from the other by shifting every letter by the same number of places in the alphabet, wrapping around from z to a. A shift by 0 is allowed, so equal strings are shift-equivalent; for example "abc" and "bcd" (shift 1) or "yza" and "abc" (shift 2).

Given the lowercase string s and a length k, consider all windows (substrings) of length k, taken at starting positions 0..n-k. Return the number of pairs of different starting positions i < j whose windows are shift-equivalent.

s = "abcbcd", k = 3
windows: abc, bcb, cbc, bcd
result = 1     (abc and bcd)
constraints: s consists of lowercase English letters
hints: Comparing every pair of windows letter by letter is far too slow: there are O(n²) pairs, each costing O(k).
Two windows are shift-equivalent exactly when their sequences of differences between neighbouring letters (modulo 26) are identical. Why does the common shift disappear in the differences?
Turn every window into a canonical key: the tuple (or bytes) of its k - 1 neighbour differences modulo 26. Count how many windows share each key; a key seen c times contributes c (c - 1) / 2 pairs.
editorial: If window B is window A shifted by d, all neighbour differences (A[x+1] - A[x]) mod 26 are equal for both, because the shift cancels in a difference. Conversely, if two windows have equal difference sequences, then every letter of one differs from the corresponding letter of the other by the same amount as the first letters do, so they are shift-equivalent. The difference sequence is therefore a complete canonical form.

Compute the difference array of the whole string once, diff[x] = (s[x+1] - s[x]) mod 26, and use the slice diff[i : i+k-1] (as a bytes object or a rolling hash) as the key of the window starting at i. Group windows with a hash map and add c(c-1)/2 for every group of size c. With slices as keys the cost is O(n k) memory-bound work, with a rolling hash it becomes O(n). For k = 1 every window has an empty key, so all windows are equivalent and the answer is C(n, 2).
time: O(n * k) with slice keys, O(n) with rolling hash
space: O(n * k) worst case with slice keys, O(n) with hashing
